text: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) acts as a covalent inhibitor of Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) by acetylating the conserved cysteine residue (Cys481) within the enzyme's active site, effectively blocking the ATP-binding pocket. This irreversible modification prevents the downstream phosphorylation of PLCγ2, thereby disrupting the B-cell receptor (BCR) signaling pathway essential for the survival and proliferation of malignant B-cells in lymphomas. While Aspirin exhibits lower binding affinity and potency compared to specialized covalent inhibitors like ibrutinib, its ability to suppress BTK-mediated oncogenic signaling provides a potential therapeutic rationale for repurposing it as an adjuvant to mitigate BCR-driven lymphomagenesis.
